Proposer 2: responder1 is seat 1 (gets offer_a), responder2 is seat 3
Draw removes one value from the proposer's pot list
Full game of rejections empties every pot list; all tied at 0 share the win
Only the proposer is asked for amounts; responders never see a number question
Offer_b range is limited to 130 - offer_a
Both responders answer; proposer is not asked to respond

flags: always taking the first option as seat 1 wins 100% of decided matches against random seats
always taking the first option as seat 2 wins 100% of decided matches against random seats

spec_choices.why: The designer fixed the table at 3. The Proposer order, the two-Responder structure and the 4 proposals each over 12 rounds only work with exactly 3 seats. The strategy is to infer the hidden pot from the offer size and from which values the Proposer has already used, to bluff about the pot in talk, and to decide whether to undercut a fellow Responder, since one acceptance is enough for the deal to pass.

spec_choices.what: Talk is a simultaneous poll broadcast to all
spec_choices.why: The source requires all three messages to be written at the same time, unseen, and then shown to everyone. The players also disagree about the split, so talk earns its place.

spec_choices.what: The pot lists are hidden table attributes (visibility none)
spec_choices.why: If the remaining lists were public, they would show the drawn pot the moment it is removed. Their contents are announced at setup, and every used value is revealed at the end of each round, so players can still track what remains, as the source intends.

spec_choices.what: The offer is asked as two sequential numbers, with b's range limited to 130 - a
spec_choices.why: A question takes one number, and limiting b's range enforces a + b <= 130 by arithmetic.

simplifications.what: A tie for the highest score is a shared win rather than a draw
simplifications.why: The engine ranks by one expression and has players level at the top share the win, with no separate draw outcome. A sole leader still wins outright, as in the source.

variation.original_summary: A two-player, one-shot bargain. A Proposer offers the Responder a share S of 100 units. If the Responder accepts, the split stands; if the Responder rejects, both get nothing.

review.evidence: The original game fails. Under 'higher total wins' with two players only the difference counts. A Responder should reject any S below 50, and a Proposer offering exactly 50 can at worst draw, so 'offer 50' never loses and 'reject below 50' never loses. The game collapses to a forced 50/50 draw, and the Proposer seat is decided by that one rule. The previous 3-player variation fixed the proposal rounds: 0/0 offers get rejected, over-offers lose, always-accept is exploited, and always-reject falls behind accepters. But its round-10 Split Demand let a leader demand 60 and never fall behind.

The original is one decision with a known pie, so there is no gap for skill to exploit. In the previous variation, players drew 3 of 4 pot values, which gave pot totals of 270 to 330. Under both sensible strategies (fixed offers, or offering a third of the pot each), the winner was whoever left out the lowest value, or the tie-break went to whoever drew small pots. Luck decided.

The original is solved instantly at 50/50. The 3-player hidden-pot version does have room to improve: reading the pot from the offer and the remaining list, playing one Responder off the other, and choosing when to reject to cut down a leader.

In the original the pie, the offer and the rules are all public, so there is nothing to infer. The previous variation added a hidden pot, but the deal decided the result, so the inference did not decide the winner.
All payoffs are sums and differences of announced numbers. The winner is the highest total, by arithmetic.

The original is text-only and turn-based but is a single move. The previous variation fit the limits only if the pot lists were game lists, and it needed a special round 10 with its own per-step conditions.

problems: P1: In the original 2-player 'higher total wins' setting, 'offer 50' and 'reject below 50' can never lose, so the game is a forced draw.
P2: The original has no hidden information and only one move, so there is nothing to infer and nothing to plan.
P3: In the previous variation, each player played only 3 of 4 pot values, so total pie differed by up to 60 points and decided the winner under good play (the lottery trap).
P4: The previous tie-break, highest Responder-gains tally, rose as one's own drawn pots fell, so the draw also decided ties.
P5: The previous Split Demand round 10 was a safe-option collapse. Demanding 60 was never behind, which locked in the leader and let anyone block at no cost.
P6: Last-proposer edge: P3 alone made the final proposal with full knowledge of the scores, and P1 alone proposed first with the least information.
P7: The attribute count was over 20 unless the pot lists were stated to be game lists.

changes.what: Three players. A proposal passes if at least one of two Responders accepts, and a rejected share is burned.
changes.why: With three players one rival's gain is not the other's loss. Two Responders compete for the offer, and a lone holdout punishes the Proposer only partly, so offering the minimum, rejecting everything or offering a fair split can each lose.

changes.what: The pot is hidden from the Responders. Each player has the list 70/90/110/130 and is told the pot only when it is drawn; the pot is revealed after the round.
changes.why: Responders must infer the pot from the offer size and from the values the Proposer has not yet played.

changes.what: 12 proposal rounds. Each player proposes exactly 4 times and plays every pot value once; only the order is random.
changes.why: Every player's pie is exactly 400, so the deal changes only what is known, not who is ahead. Under symmetric fair play everyone ends on 400 and the game is a draw.

changes.what: The tie-break is removed. A tie for the highest total is a draw.
changes.why: No tie-break that depends on the draw.

changes.what: The Split Demand round is removed entirely.
changes.why: It was a never-behind safe option. The final proposal rounds still let Responders retaliate, and a leading Responder who rejects can be overtaken if the other accepts.

changes.what: Snake proposer order: P1, P2, P3, P3, P2, P1, P1, P2, P3, P3, P2, P1.
changes.why: P1 proposes both first (least information) and last (most information). P3 proposes twice in a row in the middle, and P2's turns are evenly spread, so first-mover and last-mover effects offset.

changes.what: The pot lists are kept as game lists, not player attributes.
changes.why: This keeps the attribute count at 9.

keeps: A Proposer splits a pie and Responders accept or reject, with rejection destroying value.
The Proposer keeps the pie minus the offer, and a Responder gets the offer only by accepting.
The tension between the fairness threat (rejection) and greed (a low offer).
The hidden pie size from the previous variation, and inferring it from the offer and the remaining list.
Simultaneous non-binding talk before each offer.

recommendation.reason: The hidden-pot, three-player ultimatum has real inference and coalition play. Equalising the pies, removing the demand round and using a snake order fix every failed check within the limits.

variation.name: Hidden Pie Ultimatum III
variation.summary: Three players take turns proposing how to split a pot whose size only the Proposer knows. Every player plays each of the pot values 70, 90, 110 and 130 exactly once, in random order. One acceptance passes a deal; a rejected share is burned. Highest total after 12 rounds wins.
variation.rules:
SETUP: Three players, P1, P2 and P3, each start with a score of 0. Each player has a pot list (a game list, not a player attribute) holding the four values 70, 90, 110 and 130. Everyone knows the contents of every list.

ROUNDS: There are 12 proposal rounds. The Proposer by round is:
- rounds 1-3: P1, P2, P3
- rounds 4-6: P3, P2, P1
- rounds 7-9: P1, P2, P3
- rounds 10-12: P3, P2, P1
Each player proposes exactly 4 times. The other two players are that round's Responders; the first Responder is the one with the lower seat number.

EACH ROUND:
1. Draw: one value is drawn at random from the Proposer's remaining pot list and removed from it. This is the pot. Only the Proposer is told it. Because each list loses one value per proposal, every player plays all four values exactly once.
2. Talk: every player writes one short message at the same time, without seeing the others. Then all three messages are shown to everyone. Messages are not binding and may be false.
3. Offer: the Proposer announces two whole numbers: a for the first Responder and b for the second. Each must be 0 or more, and a + b must be at most 130. The offer is shown to everyone; the pot is not.
4. Response: both Responders choose Accept or Reject at the same time, without seeing each other's choice.
5. Scoring:
   - If at least one Responder accepts, the deal passes. The Proposer gains pot - a - b; if a + b exceeds the pot, this is negative and the Proposer loses points. Each Responder who accepted gains their offered amount. A Responder who rejected gains 0, and their share is destroyed (the Proposer still pays it).
   - If both Responders reject, the deal fails and all three gain 0 this round.
6. Reveal: the pot, both responses and all three scores are announced.

END: The game ends after round 12.
variation.objective: After round 12, the player with the strictly highest total score wins. If two or three players tie for the highest total, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Pie luck is gone: every player proposes pots totalling 400, so differences come only from bargaining. Responders must judge from the offer and the remaining list whether the hidden pot is large or small. A player's last-remaining value is public, so inference sharpens as the game goes on. Players disagree about who gets the Responder share and who gets squeezed, and only one player can win. In talk, two players may propose a pact (high offers to each other, low to the third). The excluded player tries to break it by bidding more to one partner. A player who simply follows a pact can lose: the partner may take high offers and then give low ones, or simply finish ahead. Late in the game a leading Responder must decide whether to reject. Rejecting alone does not stop the deal if the other Responder accepts, so the leader can be passed. No simple policy is safe. Offering 0/0 gets rejected and earns 0 on your own pots. Over-offering loses points. Always-accept is exploited with offers of 0 or 1. Always-reject earns only from your own proposals and falls behind. Symmetric fair play ends in a 400/400/400 draw, not a lottery.

balanced.evidence:
RESPONDER DECISION (Proposer offers a,b; pot p). Payoffs (P, R1, R2) by (R1,R2) response: (A,A) = (p-a-b, a, b); (A,R) = (p-a-b, a, 0); (R,A) = (p-a-b, 0, b); (R,R) = (0, 0, 0). A lone reject changes nothing for the Proposer and only costs the rejecter their share, so a veto works only when both reject. That makes talk meaningful. No option is strictly better: rejecting a 0 offer costs nothing and, if the other Responder also rejects, removes the Proposer's whole pot.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES. 'Offer (0,0), always accept': against itself everyone ends on 300, a draw. Against sensible Responders who jointly veto low offers it keeps about 0 per proposal and loses. Against random Responders it passes 75% of the time and keeps about 225 in expectation, which beats random, as it should. 'Always reject' never gains as a Responder and loses to anyone who gets deals through. No policy never loses. So far this is fine.

THE FLAW IS STRUCTURAL. Every player's pot list is {60, 100, 140}, summing to 300. Take any symmetric stationary policy: keep share k of the pot and give share g to each Responder. Every player then ends on exactly 300k + 2·300g, whatever order the pots come in. With even splits (p/3 each), every player finishes on exactly 300 and the game is a three-way draw every time. Sensible symmetric play converges to a draw, not a win.

SEAT EDGE (round 9). By round 9 everyone knows P3's pot exactly, because only one value is left. Suppose all are tied at T and the pot is 100. Any deal a Responder accepts that lets P3 move ahead turns the tie into a loss for them. If both reject, the result is a draw. P3 can only pass a deal by giving one Responder a winning share, for example a = 51 for P1, leaving P3 49, which makes P1 the winner. So from a tie the last Proposer can draw or play kingmaker but can never win. P1 and P2 make their final proposals while play still follows. That is a seat asymmetry, and it creates a kingmaker endgame: when P3 is behind, P3 decides which of the others wins.

playable.evidence: Within limits: 13 steps, 3 choice steps (talk, offer, response), 14 attributes, 1 hidden element, 1 draw, 9 rounds. Talk is simultaneous, and it belongs here. The Proposer and the Responders disagree about the split. The two Responders must coordinate a joint veto, and they also compete with each other, so following a proposal can cost a player. Responses are a simultaneous poll. Scoring is arithmetic using `when` conditions on the accept count. The game is finite. It needs no judge, board or clock. One gap: the rules do not say what happens if the Proposer enters a + b > pot. The engine must validate this against the hidden pot, or the rules should say 'such an offer is replaced by (0,0)'. In the endgame, cooperation (passing deals) still matters, because a joint veto is the tool; it is not dominated by a safe option.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Chance is close to zero. Each player's pots always total 300, so the draw affects only the order of pots and what is hidden when. Hidden information shrinks over the game: in rounds 1-3 the pot is one of 3 values, in rounds 4-6 one of 2, and in rounds 7-9 it is known. Offers reveal information, since a + b ≤ pot means an offer of 130 proves the pot is 140. Responders can act on this by vetoing offers they infer are stingy. Coalition reading, bluffing in talk and tracking scores decide the result. With equal good play the result is a deterministic draw, not a random one. That is a balance problem rather than a luck problem.

required_changes: Break the deterministic three-way draw. For example, add a tiebreak computed by arithmetic, such as 'among tied players, the one with the higher total gained as a Responder wins; if still tied, the game is a draw'. Alternatively, give each player 4 pot values (e.g. 70, 90, 110, 130) of which only 3 are drawn, so totals differ modestly and the last pot is never certain.

Remove the last-Proposer kingmaker edge. Either make the round-9 pot uncertain (with the 4-value list above), or add a final round 10 in which all three players simultaneously propose a split of a common public pot of 60 and the median proposal is applied, so no single seat ends the game as the vetoed Proposer.
State the handling of an invalid offer (a + b > pot): it is replaced by (0,0), or rejected and re-entered.

balanced.evidence: WINNER RULE applied to round 10 (Split Demand). Pie 60, demands 0-60, all 0 if the total exceeds 60. Policy 'always demand 60' against any opponent demands x, y: if x = y = 0, the total is 60, so you gain +60 and they gain 0. If x + y > 0, the total exceeds 60, so all three gain 0. Round-10 gain table for 'demand 60' against (x, y): (0,0) gives me +60 and them 0. Any other pair gives 0 to all. That policy is never behind in round 10, so it never loses ground. For whoever leads after round 9, demanding 60 locks in the win. A trailing player cannot get anything if the leader does this. Any player can also demand 60 at no relative cost, purely to block. The round is a safe-option collapse: cooperating (20/20/20) cannot beat it, which is exactly the excluded pattern. Proposal-round policies are not dominant. 'Always offer 0/0': at an offer of 0, Reject weakly dominates Accept for a Responder, because accepting gains 0 and lets the proposer take the whole pot. Sensible Responders both reject, so the proposer gets 0 three times and loses. 'Always offer 65/65': the proposer gains pot - 130, which is 0 or less, and loses. 'Responder always accepts': a sensible proposer offers that player 1 and the other 0. That gives the proposer about pot - 1, so the always-acceptor loses. 'Always reject': gains come only from your own proposals, and you lose to accepters. So the proposal phase is fine, but round 10 fails the check. Seat edge: P3 makes the last proposal (round 9) with full knowledge of the scores, and round 10 offers no way to retaliate against it. P1 proposes first, while it has the least information about the other pots. This edge is moderate.

playable.evidence: Limits: steps 11, choice steps 3 in proposal rounds (talk, offer, response) and 2 in round 10, hidden elements 1, draws 1 per round, rounds 10. All are within limits. Round 10 can be built with per-step `when round==10` conditions, which the engine supports. Attributes: 3 scores + 3 tallies + 12 pot-list values already make 18, before the current pot, a, b and the responses. The claimed 17 holds only if the pot lists are game lists rather than attributes. This needs stating, but it is fixable. Talk is simultaneous, and in proposal rounds it is well placed: Responders have opposed interests (who gets a, who gets b) and a shared interest in a joint rejection. Rules are complete: overpaying is defined, the case where only one Responder accepts is defined, and the tie-break chain ends in a draw. Repeated-game check failure: the game has a fixed length and is decided by highest total, and in the last round the safe option (demand 60) wins outright for the leader. Cooperation in round 10 never pays, so round-10 talk only adds words.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Pot luck: each player draws 3 of {70, 90, 110, 130}, so their pot total ranges from 270 (unused 130) to 330 (unused 70). The mean is 300 and the spread is 60. Intended good play, case A, fixed offers based on the expected pot (say 30/30): proposer score = own pot total - 180 + 6×30 (received as Responder) = own pot total. The winner is whoever left out the lowest value, which is the random draw alone. Case B, proportional thirds (offer pot/3 to each Responder): every player's total = (sum of all nine pots)/3, so all are tied. The tie-break is the Responder-gains tally = (others' pots)/3, which is highest for the player whose own pots were smallest. Again pure luck decides. Round 10 adds nothing (20/20/20 is a wash, or 0 for all). Between near-equal skilled players, the 60-point pie difference, or a tie-break driven by the draw, decides the result. Something real can be inferred: the hidden pot from the size of the offer and the remaining list, and the other Responder's likely rejection. But good play does not overcome the deal, because the deal itself picks the winner.

required_changes: Equalise the pie. Have each player play all four pot values: 12 proposal rounds, each player proposing 4 times, so everyone's pot total is 400. Only the order is random, and the hidden-pot inference from the remaining list is kept.

Replace the tie-break 'highest Responder-gains tally', which is inversely tied to the drawn pots, with one that does not depend on the draw. For example, use fewest proposals rejected, or simply call it a draw.

Remove the Split Demand round, or redesign it so that over-demanding has a relative cost. For example, if the total exceeds 60, the excess is subtracted from the highest demander only, and the rest gain their demands scaled down. Show that no demand is never-behind for the leader.

Offset the last-proposer edge. For example, end with a final simultaneous round, or give each seat the final proposal across a rotation, so that P3 does not alone propose last with full information and no retaliation.
State that the pot lists are kept as game lists (or table attributes) so the attribute count stays within 20.

balanced.evidence:
Each player proposes exactly 4 times and draws each of 70, 90, 110 and 130 exactly once, so every player handles 400 units in total. Chance changes only the order of the pots, not the total.

Responder payoffs per round, with offer (a, b), pot V, and 'other' meaning the other Responder:
- Both accept: Proposer V-a-b, R1 a, R2 b.
- R1 accepts, R2 rejects: Proposer V-a-b, R1 a, R2 0 (b is destroyed).
- R1 rejects, R2 accepts: Proposer V-a-b, R1 0, R2 b.
- Both reject: all 0.
A lone rejection costs only the rejecter. Denying the Proposer requires both Responders to reject, and Responders are rivals for the single win. No Responder option dominates, because accepting raises both your own score and the Proposer's.

WINNER RULE applied to the thoughtless policies:
(1) Proposer always offers (0,0). Under the winner rule, Responders who reason lose nothing by both rejecting, so the Proposer gets 0 in all 4 rounds. Meanwhile the other two pay each other positive offers. Against sensible play this policy loses. Against random Responders (each accepts with probability 0.5) the deal passes 75% of the time, about 300 in expectation, so it can win against random play only. It does not 'never lose'.
(2) Proposer always offers the maximum, e.g. 65/65. Net 400-520 = -120 from proposing, while handing 130 per round to rivals. It almost always loses.
(3) Responder always accepts. A Proposer offers it (1,0) and keeps V-1, so this player is exploitable and loses to sensible play.
(4) Responder always rejects. It earns nothing as a Responder. Proposers simply pay the other Responder, so this player's total comes only from its own proposals and it trails. It loses.
(5) Fixed split on the mean pot, 33/33. Proposer net 400-264 = 136 plus receipts. This is a symmetric baseline that beats neither a pot-adaptive player nor a bluffer reliably.
No policy never loses.

Seats: the mirrored order gives P1 rounds 1, 6, 7, 12; P2 rounds 2, 5, 8, 11; P3 rounds 3, 4, 9, 10. Each player's 4th pot is publicly deducible, in rounds 12, 11 and 10 respectively, so the information is symmetric. P1 proposes last with no retaliation to fear, but the Responders also act last and can jointly veto, so neither side has a clear edge. All three players can realistically win. No mislabelled payoff ordering was found.

playable.evidence:
Complexity against the limits:
- steps 12 (limit 20)
- choice steps 3: talk, offer, response (limit 4)
- attributes 9 (limit 20)
- hidden elements 1: the pot (limit 3)
- random draws 1 per round (limit 1)
- rounds 12 (limit 40)

The draw from a per-player game list uses the supported shared_deck_draw workaround (remove/append). The conditional payouts use arithmetic `when`/`if`; no block branching is needed. Responses are a simultaneous poll, the offer is a numeric bid pair, and the game ends after a fixed 12 rounds with an arithmetic winner rule. There is no board, judge, clock, trading or binding agreement.

Talk is simultaneous and opens every round. That fits here: the three players have conflicting interests, a Proposer can bluff the pot, and Responders can coordinate a joint veto or court one another. Following a proposal can be costly.

Minor gap: the rules do not say what happens to an offer with a+b>130 or negative numbers. A referee or input bound can enforce this, so it is not a failure.

There is no cooperate/defect structure in which the safe option wins every late round. The final rounds still involve live veto and bargaining decisions.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Every player plays the same four pots, so chance affects only when each pot arrives, and therefore how much is hidden. I estimate under about 15% of the outcome comes from chance.

If all three play the same pot-dependent strategy, their totals are identical and the game is a draw. The random order does not decide the winner, so the 'luck decides under equal play' failure does not apply.

There is real inference:
- In a player's 1st proposal the pot is one of 4 values. Inference from the offer and the talk matters: offering 40/40 on a 70 pot costs 10, while on a 130 pot it nets 50.
- In the 2nd proposal the pot is one of 3 values.
- In the 3rd proposal the pot is one of 2 values, a 50/50 bluff spot.
- The 4th proposal has a public pot.

Players must also model the opponents in a three-way race: whether to join a veto, whether a partner will defect from it, and how much to pay a trailing Responder. A player who reasons well (pot inference, veto timing, standings-aware offers) is clearly favoured over a thoughtless one.

design_flags_left: always taking the first option as seat 1 wins 100% of decided matches against random seats
always taking the first option as seat 2 wins 100% of decided matches against random seats

triage.reason: In every failing scenario the move log shows both Responders answering 'Accept', not 'Reject'. The game then correctly paid the Proposer pot - a - b, which gives 70+90+110+130 = 400 each over a full game, 130 in round 1 and +70 in the round-12 case. The game follows the rules; the tests assumed rejections they never actually scripted, since the 'decline' default resolved to Accept.
triage.guidance: When a scenario depends on both Responders rejecting, script that explicitly. Add rules for each Responder seat that choose the 'Reject' option every time it is offered, instead of relying on the 'decline' default, which here picked Accept. Then expect all three scores to stay 0, matching the rule for a failed deal. For the full-game R8 check, also assert that pots_p1, pots_p2 and pots_p3 are empty (length 0) and that each seat proposed 4 times. For the round-12 ending test, with both Responders scripted to Reject, the given scores stay unchanged and the winner follows from them. Do not let any expected score depend on which pot value is drawn, because the draw is random. Asserting only the score delta of the Proposer is fine only when the offer is accepted and the pot is known; otherwise assert that the scores are unchanged. For R10, a talk-only test should script rejections, or should not assert scores at all. The point of R10 is that the round completes after the simultaneous talk, so assert round/proposer progression rather than a score.

triage.reason: The game file is correct; the design is degenerate. A single Accept passes the deal and rejecting never costs a Responder anything, so offering 0/0 keeps nearly the whole pot and accepting is never worse than rejecting, which is why the 'first option' policy wins every decided match and the 'last option' policy loses every one.
triage.guidance:
Remove the near-dominant 'offer the minimum, always accept' play.
1. Require BOTH Responders to accept for the deal to pass, so a lowball offer can be vetoed by either Responder. Otherwise, give a lone rejecter real power, for example a single rejection voids the Proposer's gain.
2. Make rejection a meaningful threat. Add a rule where an ungenerous offer is punished, such as a minimum total offer tied to the largest pot, or a Proposer penalty when the deal fails, so that offering 0 is risky.
3. Make the stingiest and most generous ends of the offer range both risky, so neither the first nor the last listed option is reliably good or bad.
4. Check the seat balance. Seat 3 won far less often even against random play, so re-examine the proposer order and the responder ordering (the 'first Responder' is always the lower seat) for structural seat advantages.
5. Re-test with simple fixed policies to confirm no single choice dominates.
